title: Sentence formation
summary: The two basic word orders, and how to turn one into the other
goals: Tell the two word orders apart: subject-predicate (with ay) and inverted
Know the two jobs of ay
Turn a subject-predicate sentence into the inverted order
Use mga with plural subjects in the inverted order, and shorten at to 't

sections.title: Two ways to build a sentence

blocks.t: There are **two basic ways** to form a sentence in Tagalog:

head: Word order
Pattern
Emphasis on
rows: predicate + subject (the subject may also be left out)
blocks.title: The two word orders
The same sentence both ways
blocks.note: The house is big. Ay is not used in the inverted order.

blocks.title: Which is more common?
blocks.t: Tagalog speakers tend to use the **inverted** word order more often in everyday speech.

A sentence is in this order when the **subject is the most important element** and comes first. The word **ay** (like the English *is* and *are*) is used. The speaker wants to focus attention on the subject.

items.tl: Sina Peter at Mary ay mga batà.
Ang babáe at ang laláki ay naglúlutò.
items.en: The woman and the man are cooking.

head: Job
In the sentences
What it does
rows: Ang báhay ay malakí. Si Peter ay mabaít. Sina Peter at Mary ay mga batà.
links the subject to what is said about it (is, are)
Ang batà ay kumákain. Ang babáe at ang laláki ay naglúlutò.
goes with the principal verb, which is the chief action (is eating, are cooking)
blocks.title: Ay
Action words
blocks.t: **Kumákain** (is/are eating) and **naglúlutò** (is/are cooking) are verbs. Tagalog verbs change their form, which later lessons cover. For now, learn them as whole words.
A sentence is in the **inverted** or **transposed** order when the **predicate comes first**, before the subject. The word **ay is not used**. The focus is on the predicate rather than the subject.

items.en: Big, the house is. (The house is big.)
Eating, the child is. (The child is eating.)

blocks.t: How to turn a sentence around

head: Step
What to do
Example
rows: Move the predicate to the front
Keep the article with the subject
blocks.title: Step by step
Remember
items: **Ay** is only used in the subject-predicate order.
The article (ang, si, siná) stays with the subject.
In the inverted order, the subject comes at the end of the sentence, or may be left out.

sections.title: Plural subjects in the inverted order

blocks.t: In inverted sentences that have **plural nouns as their subjects**, the word **mga**, not **ang mga**, comes before the first noun.

items.tl: Mga batà sina Peter at Mary.
items.en: Children, Peter and Mary are. (Peter and Mary are children.)

items.tl: Mga lungsód ang Maynila at Cebu.
items.en: Cities, Manila and Cebu are. (Manila and Cebu are cities.)
Women, Helen and companions are. (Helen and companions are women.)
Animals, the dog and cat are. (The dog and cat are animals.)

blocks.title: Sina with one name
blocks.t: **Mga babáe sina Helen** uses siná with only one name. It means *Helen and her companions*.
The connective **at** (*and*) may be shortened to **'t** and attached to the word before it when that word **ends in a vowel**, such as **áso**: áso at pusà becomes **áso't pusà**.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Two word orders: subject-predicate (with ay) and inverted (no ay).
Tagalogs use the inverted order more often in everyday speech.
Ay links the subject to the predicate, or helps the main verb.
With plural subjects in the inverted order, start with mga, not ang mga.
At can become 't after a word ending in a vowel.

vocab.note: Shortened to 't after a word ending in a vowel: áso't pusà

exercises.q: Which word order do Tagalogs use more often in everyday speech?
exercises.explain: Tagalog speakers tend to use the inverted word order more often.

exercises.q: Turn around: Si Peter ay laláki.
exercises.explain: Move the predicate to the front and leave out ay.

exercises.q: Turn around: Si Ruth ay magandá.
exercises.explain: The article si stays with Ruth.

exercises.q: Turn around: Si Peter ay marúnong.
exercises.explain: Predicate first, then the article and the subject.

exercises.q: Turn around: Sina Helen at Tom ay mga batà.
options: Mga batà sina Helen at Tom.
Ang mga batà sina Helen at Tom.
Mga batà ay sina Helen at Tom.
exercises.answer: Mga batà sina Helen at Tom.
exercises.explain: Start with mga, not ang mga.

exercises.q: Turn around: Ang mga sapátos ay malilínis.
exercises.explain: Move the predicate to the front and leave out ay.

exercises.q: Which sentence is in the subject-predicate order?
exercises.explain: It has ay between the subject and the predicate.

exercises.q: What happens to ay in the inverted order?
exercises.explain: Ay only appears in the subject-predicate order.

exercises.q: In "Ang batà ay kumákain", what job does ay do?
options: A helping verb with the principal verb
exercises.answer: A helping verb with the principal verb
exercises.explain: Kumákain is the chief action, and ay goes with it.

exercises.q: In "Ang báhay ay malakí", what job does ay do?
exercises.explain: It links the subject to what is said about it.

exercises.q: In an inverted sentence with a plural subject, what comes before the first noun?
What does "Mga babáe sina Helen" mean?
exercises.explain: Siná with one name means that person and companions.

exercises.q: When can at (and) be shortened to 't?
options: After a word ending in a vowel
After a word ending in a consonant
At the start of a sentence
exercises.answer: After a word ending in a vowel
exercises.explain: áso at pusà becomes áso't pusà.

exercises.q: In which order is the focus on the predicate?
exercises.explain: The focus is on whatever comes first.

exercises.en: The woman and the man are cooking.
exercises.tl: Ang babáe at ang laláki ay naglúlutò.

exercises.en: The dog and cat are animals.

exercises.q: Match each subject-predicate sentence to its inverted form.

recap: Two word orders: subject-predicate (with ay) and inverted or transposed (no ay).
Tagalogs use the inverted order more often in everyday speech.
Ay is a linking verb (Ang báhay ay malakí) or a helping verb (Ang batà ay kumákain).
To invert: put the predicate first and leave out ay. The subject may even be left out.
Plural subject, inverted order: start with mga, not ang mga. At becomes 't after a vowel.
